finding.claim: The /users endpoint returns the users of any organization named in the client-supplied `org` query parameter. No authentication or tenant-ownership check is applied, so any caller can enumerate the id and name of every org's users (IDOR / broken access control).
finding.source: req.query.org on GET /users, attacker-controlled and sent unauthenticated
finding.sink: req.pg.query("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1") with the result returned via res.json(rows)

trace.note: app = express() is created with no auth or session middleware registered anywhere in the file
GET /users handler has no authentication or authorization guard
req.query.org is used directly as the tenant filter instead of an org derived from the authenticated principal
Matching rows are returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: The query is parameterized ($1), so there is no SQL injection. I found no app.use middleware, session or identity check, and no comparison of the org against a caller identity. req.pg is not set in this file, so an external middleware could exist, but nothing in the code shows one enforcing org scoping. The finding depends on the deployment adding no such control.

verdict.guard_found: none (the query is parameterized at db.js:9, which stops SQL injection but not the access-control issue)
verdict.reason: db.js:8-10 passes the unauthenticated req.query.org to the users query and returns the rows, and db.js is the only app file, with no app.use, session or identity check before line 8 (app.listen at db.js:23 serves it directly), so any anonymous caller can list any org's users.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (only SQL parameterization at db.js:9, which prevents injection but not cross-tenant access)
verdict_facts.reason: db.js:9 filters users by the client-supplied req.query.org with no check against the caller's identity or org anywhere in the handler (db.js:8-11) or file, so any HTTP client can read any org's user ids and names.
